detectiveClues.headline: Walking 250 Miles to Guadalupe & Sierra Gorda
detectiveClues.clueText: Landing at Veracruz in December 1749, Father Serra refused the carriage offered to him and walked all 250 rugged mountain miles to Mexico City on foot—suffering a venomous insect bite on his leg that caused a painful, open swelling for the remaining thirty-five years of his life! stops.title: Planting the First Bell at Mission San Diego de Alcalá
stops.subtitle: Sweep your lantern across Mission San Diego de Alcalá to uncover 3 hidden memories
stops.imageCaption: Crisp whitewashed Spanish colonial adobe bell wall silhouetted against brilliant Pacific blue skies and sunlit golden coastal hills.
stops.whatYouCanSeeToday: Mission San Diego de Alcalá’s iconic five-bell whitewashed adobe campanario still stands as a lively parish and California’s oldest historic mission site.
stops.didYouKnowHighlight: When frightened expedition leaders nearly voted to abandon starving San Diego and sail back to Mexico in 1770, stubborn Father Serra refused to board the ship—praying a nine-day novena to St. Joseph until the rescue supply ship *San Antonio* literally sailed over the horizon on St. Joseph’s Day, March 19!
stops.saintQuote: To speak of going back is out of the question—always forward!

Over the next fifteen years, walking thousands of coastal miles despite asthma and constant pain, he personally founded **nine** missions that birthed modern San Diego, Carmel, San Luis Obispo, San Francisco, and Santa Clara.

stops.title: Home by the Cypress Sea at Carmel Mission
stops.subtitle: Sweep your lantern across Mission San Carlos Borromeo de Carmelo to uncover 3 hidden memories
stops.ancientPlaceName: Mission San Carlos Borromeo de Carmelo
stops.imageCaption: Warm golden sandstone Moorish-domed mission basilica framed by blooming bougainvillea and gnarled cypresses overlooking the sparkling misty Pacific Ocean.
stops.whatYouCanSeeToday: Carmel Mission Basilica—widely called the jewel of California’s missions—welcomes visitors to pray beside St. Junípero Serra’s stone sanctuary tomb and step inside his preserved tiny adobe bedroom.
stops.didYouKnowHighlight: When Pope Francis canonized St. Junípero Serra in September 2015, he celebrated him as an tireless missionary who kept going forward with joy—and California’s golden sandstone Carmel Mission still rings his original bells!
stops.saintQuote: I promise you I will not forget you when I reach heaven.

hiddenArtifacts.storyUnlocked: Falling in love with the misty cypress coast and sparkling bay of Carmel, St. Junípero Serra made **Mission San Carlos Borromeo de Carmelo** his home headquarters for his final fourteen years—living in a tiny bare-walled adobe cell with a wooden plank bed and a small desk where he wrote hundreds of letters. Passing away peacefully on August 28, 1784 at age seventy, he was canonized right in Washington, D.C. in 2015—the first saint ever canonized on United States soil!

completionSummary: You journeyed from Franconia’s four-spired imperial cathedral all the way to the breezy Baltic coast with St. Otto of Bamberg—the "Apostle of Pomerania" who healed imperial feuds as a peacemaker and won northern Europe by bringing gifts, fairness, and respect instead of swords.

stops.title: Peacemaker-Bishop of Four-Spired Bamberg
stops.subtitle: Sweep your lantern across Babenberga (Bamberg Cathedral) to uncover 3 hidden memories
stops.imageCaption: Majestic four-spired pale sandstone Romanesque imperial cathedral glowing in golden Franconian light above historic timbered river houses.
stops.whatYouCanSeeToday: Bamberg’s breathtaking UNESCO Old Town and four-spired Cathedral still glow with the architectural and charitable vision St. Otto poured into Franconia.
stops.didYouKnowHighlight: During a devastating Bavarian famine, Bishop Otto refused to dine on fine food—spending the entire episcopal treasury to buy grain and personally distributing loaves so thousands of families survived!
stops.saintQuote: True authority is measured by how gently it lifts the poor.

stops.title: Breezy Baltic Voyage to Szczecin & Pomerania
stops.subtitle: Sweep your lantern across Stettin (Szczecin, Pomerania) to uncover 3 hidden memories
stops.imageCaption: Breezy amber-lit Baltic port harbor framed by timber medieval ships and tall coastal pines as a tall smiling bishop hands gifts to curious Pomeranian townspeople.
stops.whatYouCanSeeToday: Across northern Poland and northeastern Germany, St. Otto of Bamberg is cherished as the beloved **"Apostle of Pomerania"**—celebrated for proving that genuine friendship achieves what armies never could!
stops.didYouKnowHighlight: Otto deliberately arrived in Pomerania dressed cleanly and generously paying his own way—because earlier beggared missionaries had been mocked as fortune-hunters! His thoughtful cultural sensitivity won entire cities overnight!
stops.saintQuote: We have not come to take your silver, but to share a treasure that can never be stolen.

hiddenArtifacts.foundTitle: Breezy Baltic Voyage to Szczecin & Pomerania
hiddenArtifacts.storyUnlocked: When Polish Duke Bolesław III begged someone to preach the Gospel to the fiercely independent Baltic Pomeranians—where earlier harsh preachers had failed completely!—sixty-four-year-old Bishop Otto stepped forward with a genius strategy: **never ask for a single coin, and come bringing generous gifts, fair trade, and total respect!** Speaking fluent Slavic, redeeming captives from slavery, and arriving with wagonloads of fine cloth and provisions for the poor, Otto peacefully baptized over 22,000 Pomeranians across Szczecin, Wolin, and Pyrzyce!

detectiveClues.headline: Hilltop Resting Place at St. Michael’s Abbey, Bamberg
detectiveClues.clueText: Returning home to Bamberg after two legendary Baltic missionary journeys, elderly Bishop Otto kept founding hospitals, restoring churches, and writing letters of encouragement to his newborn Pomeranian parishes right until his peaceful passing on June 30, 1139. Canonized fifty years later, he rests inside his beloved hilltop Abbey of St. Michael overlooking the valley he loved.

trailSubtitle: 6 Stops · Jerusalem, Kerala, Chennai & Italy
globeHeaderSubtitle: Sacred Trails of St. Thomas (Upper Room to India & Ortona)
completionSummary: You traced St. Thomas the Apostle’s footsteps from the Upper Room in Jerusalem across the Arabian Sea to Kodungallur and Palayoor in Kerala, Little Mount and San Thome in Chennai, India, and the Basilica of his relics in Ortona, Italy.

stops.title: The Upper Room & The Wounds of Christ
stops.subtitle: Explore the stone Cenacle of Mount Zion where St. Thomas proclaimed “My Lord and my God!”
stops.imageCaption: Vaulted limestone arches of the Cenacle (Upper Room) on Mount Zion in Jerusalem.
stops.whatYouCanSeeToday: Just outside Zion Gate on the southern crest of Jerusalem’s Old City, pilgrims can climb the stone steps into the medieval vaulted Cenacle (Upper Room), venerated since the early Church as the site of the Last Supper, Pentecost, and Christ’s appearance to St. Thomas.
stops.didYouKnowHighlight: Though remembered as “Doubting Thomas,” his exclamation upon seeing the Risen Christ—“My Lord and my God!” (John 20:28)—is actually the single boldest, clearest confession of Jesus’s divinity spoken by anyone in all four Gospels!
stops.saintQuote: “Thomas answered and said to Him: ‘My Lord and my God!’” — John 20:28
stops.detectiveCaseTitle: Case #1 · The Stone Upper Room Where Doubt Turned to Boldest Faith
stops.detectiveLeadPrompt: Read the 3 detective clues below, then rotate and zoom into the ancient hilltop city on the 3D Globe where St. Thomas touched the Risen Christ’s wounds before setting out for the East.

detectiveClues.headline: A Golden-Stone Hilltop Sanctuary Outside Zion Gate
detectiveClues.clueText: Perched between the Mediterranean Sea and the Dead Sea, this walled holy city requires golden limestone on every building facade. On Mount Zion just south of its Old City walls stands the medieval vaulted Cenacle (Upper Room).

detectiveClues.headline: Why “Doubting Thomas” Spoke the Highest Confession in the Gospels!
detectiveClues.clueText: While people call him "Doubting Thomas," his four-word cry in this room—"My Lord and my God!" (John 20:28)—is the only time in all four Gospels that an Apostle directly addresses Jesus as both Lord and God!

detectiveClues.headline: Eight Days After Easter in the Upper Room (33 AD)
detectiveClues.clueText: Eight days after the Resurrection, Jesus appeared through locked doors here and invited Thomas to place his finger into the nail marks. When the Apostles cast lots for their mission fields, Thomas received the distant lands of Parthia and India.

hiddenArtifacts.riddleToFind: Center of the vaulted limestone hall bathed in warm shafts of sunlight.
hiddenArtifacts.hintDirection: Click marker #1 in the sunlit center of the stone Upper Room.
hiddenArtifacts.foundTitle: Eight Days After Easter: “My Lord and My God!” (John 20:28)
hiddenArtifacts.storyUnlocked: Absent on Easter Sunday evening, Thomas declared he would not believe unless he saw the nail marks. Eight days later in this Upper Room, Christ stood before him—and Thomas uttered the supreme confession of faith: "My Lord and my God!"
hiddenArtifacts.stoneKeyMeaning: Thomas’s supreme confession of Christ’s divinity in the Upper Room

hiddenArtifacts.riddleToFind: The ancient stone columns and ribbed Crusader arches supporting the upper floor.
hiddenArtifacts.hintDirection: Click marker #2 on the stone pillar and gothic vaulting.
hiddenArtifacts.foundTitle: Where Is It Modern Day Now? Mount Zion, Jerusalem
hiddenArtifacts.storyUnlocked: Today the Cenacle stands on Mount Zion just outside the Zion Gate of Jerusalem’s Old City. Rebuilt with gothic ribbed vaults by Franciscan friars in the 14th century over early Judeo-Christian synagogue foundations, it remains open to pilgrims daily.
hiddenArtifacts.stoneKeyMeaning: The hilltop sanctuary where the Cenacle stands today

hiddenArtifacts.riddleToFind: The arched stone window looking out toward the eastern horizon.
hiddenArtifacts.hintDirection: Click marker #3 near the sunlit stone window on the right.
hiddenArtifacts.foundTitle: Did You Know? The Apostle Who Traveled Farther Than Any Other!
hiddenArtifacts.storyUnlocked: Known in Aramaic as Toma ("The Twin") and in Greek as Didymus, St. Thomas traveled farther outside the Roman Empire than any other of the Twelve Apostles—journeying across Mesopotamia and the Arabian Sea all the way to southern India!
hiddenArtifacts.stoneKeyMeaning: The Greek name of the Apostle who carried the Gospel beyond the Roman Empire to India

stops.title: Landing on the Spice Coast of Muziris
stops.subtitle: Trace the monsoon trade winds to the Malabar harbor where St. Thomas landed in 52 AD
stops.eraLabel: 52 AD · Arrival on the Malabar Coast
stops.imageCaption: Palm-lined Malabar backwaters of Kodungallur, Kerala (ancient Muziris), where St. Thomas landed in 52 AD.
stops.whatYouCanSeeToday: Today, ancient Muziris is the serene Malabar coast town of Kodungallur in Kerala’s Thrissur district, India. On the banks of the Periyar estuary at Azhikode stands the Mar Thoma Pontifical Shrine, marking the harbor where St. Thomas stepped ashore in 52 AD and preserving the relic of his right arm bone.
stops.didYouKnowHighlight: For centuries, skeptics wondered if 1st-century ships could sail directly from the Roman Middle East to Kerala—until recent excavations at Pattanam (ancient Muziris) unearthed thousands of 1st-century Roman wine amphorae and Augustus Caesar gold coins!
stops.saintQuote: “Go into the whole world and proclaim the Gospel to every creature.” — Mark 16:15
stops.detectiveCaseTitle: Case #2 · The Lost Roman Spice Port of the Malabar Backwaters
stops.detectiveLeadPrompt: Sailing with the summer monsoon winds across the Arabian Sea in 52 AD, which legendary black-pepper harbor on India’s southwestern Malabar Coast welcomed St. Thomas ashore?

detectiveClues.headline: A River-Estuary Town in Thrissur District, Kerala, India
detectiveClues.clueText: Called Muziris by the Romans and Shingly by medieval travelers, today this lush backwater town in Kerala, southwestern India, hosts the Mar Thoma Pontifical Shrine where the Periyar River meets the Arabian Sea.

detectiveClues.headline: 1st-Century Roman Gold Coins & Amphorae Proved His Sea Route!
detectiveClues.clueText: Roman historian Pliny the Elder called this port "the first emporium of India"—just a 40-day monsoon sail from the Red Sea. Modern digs here unearthed thousands of 1st-century Roman amphorae and imperial coins from the exact era Thomas landed!

detectiveClues.headline: Landing at Maliankara in 52 AD & Founding the Seven Churches
detectiveClues.clueText: Arriving on a merchant vessel in 52 AD, St. Thomas was welcomed by the local Chera king and Jewish spice traders, establishing the first of Kerala’s historic "Ezharappallikal" (Seven and a Half Churches).

hiddenArtifacts.riddleToFind: The traditional wooden spice boat moored along the golden river estuary.
hiddenArtifacts.hintDirection: Click marker #1 on the wooden vessel in the harbor.
hiddenArtifacts.foundTitle: Sailing the Hippalus Monsoon Winds to India (52 AD)
hiddenArtifacts.storyUnlocked: In the 1st century AD, Greek and Roman navigators harnessed the seasonal southwest monsoon winds (Hippalus) to sail straight across the Arabian Sea in 40 days. St. Thomas boarded a spice ship with the merchant Habban and landed here at Muziris in 52 AD.
hiddenArtifacts.stoneKeyMeaning: The ancient spice port where St. Thomas first landed in India

hiddenArtifacts.riddleToFind: The carved granite cross and traditional oil lamp on the stone wharf.
hiddenArtifacts.hintDirection: Click marker #2 on the stone wharf in the right foreground.
hiddenArtifacts.foundTitle: Did You Know? The Pattanam Roman Treasure Digs!
hiddenArtifacts.storyUnlocked: Recent archaeological excavations at nearby Pattanam uncovered Roman terra sigillata pottery, Mediterranean glass beads, and 1st-century coins—proving vibrant daily contact between the Mediterranean world and Kerala during St. Thomas’s lifetime!
hiddenArtifacts.stoneKeyMeaning: The seven and a half early Christian communities founded by St. Thomas in Kerala

hiddenArtifacts.riddleToFind: The palm-fringed shoreline looking toward the modern Pontifical Shrine.
hiddenArtifacts.hintDirection: Click marker #3 along the palm-lined distant shore.
hiddenArtifacts.foundTitle: Where Is It Modern Day Now? Kodungallur, Kerala, India
hiddenArtifacts.storyUnlocked: Today, ancient Muziris (later called Cranganore) is Kodungallur in Kerala’s Thrissur district. In 1953, Cardinal Eugene Tisserant brought a bone relic of St. Thomas’s right arm from Ortona, Italy back to the Mar Thoma Pontifical Shrine here!
hiddenArtifacts.stoneKeyMeaning: Modern-day Malabar coastal town where ancient Muziris stands today

stops.title: The Baptismal Pond of the Malabar Scholars
stops.subtitle: Visit India’s oldest continuous church and the lotus pond where St. Thomas baptized the first families
stops.imageCaption: St. Thomas Syro-Malabar Pilgrim Church and historic baptismal pond at Palayoor, Kerala, India.
stops.whatYouCanSeeToday: In modern Palayoor (near Guruvayur in Thrissur district, Kerala), you can visit St. Thomas Major Archiepiscopal Pilgrim Church—the oldest continuously active church in India, established in 52 AD—and stand beside the preserved Thaliyakulam Pond where St. Thomas baptized local Namboothiri scholars.
stops.didYouKnowHighlight: Around the church courtyard in Palayoor, you can still see ancient carved granite Hindu temple stones, a traditional brass “Kalvilakku” (stone lamp), and the Boat Jetty ("Bottiukulam") where St. Thomas arrived by backwater canoe nearly 2,000 years ago!
stops.saintQuote: “Blessed are those who have not seen and yet have believed.” — John 20:29
stops.detectiveCaseTitle: Case #3 · The Lotus Pond Baptism & India’s Oldest Active Parish
stops.detectiveLeadPrompt: Journey slightly north along Kerala’s Malabar coast to the ancient temple town where St. Thomas baptized Brahmin scholars in a lotus water tank that still exists today!

detectiveClues.headline: A Historic Pilgrim Town Next to Guruvayur in Central Kerala
detectiveClues.clueText: Located in central Kerala’s Thrissur district just two kilometers from Guruvayur, this peaceful palm-shaded town is home to the oldest continuously functioning Christian church in all of India (founded in 52 AD).

detectiveClues.headline: The Preserved “Thaliyakulam” Baptismal Pond & Ancient Stone Lamps!
detectiveClues.clueText: When local Vedic scholars threw water into the air during morning prayers in the Thaliyakulam pond, tradition says Thomas prayed that the water droplets remain suspended like glowing pearls in midair—inspiring the families to seek baptism in that very pond!

detectiveClues.headline: Origin of the Ancient St. Thomas Christian (Nasrani) Families
detectiveClues.clueText: The ancestral families baptized here by St. Thomas—including Pakalomattam, Sankarapuri, Kalli, and Kaliyankal—preserved the Syriac liturgy and apostolic faith across twenty centuries.

hiddenArtifacts.riddleToFind: The stone-stepped Thaliyakulam water tank reflecting the church facade.
hiddenArtifacts.hintDirection: Click marker #1 on the stepped water pond in the foreground.
hiddenArtifacts.foundTitle: The Thaliyakulam Baptismal Pond (52 AD)
hiddenArtifacts.storyUnlocked: Beside this tranquil stepped water tank (Thaliyakulam), St. Thomas engaged in dialogue with local Brahmin scholars performing morning ablutions, leading to the baptism of the pioneering St. Thomas Christian (Mar Thoma Nasrani) families of India.
hiddenArtifacts.stoneKeyMeaning: The preserved water tank in Palayoor where St. Thomas baptized the first families

hiddenArtifacts.riddleToFind: The carved granite oil lamp (Kalvilakku) standing in the church courtyard.
hiddenArtifacts.hintDirection: Click marker #2 on the tall stone oil lamp beside the courtyard.
hiddenArtifacts.foundTitle: Did You Know? 2,000 Years of Unbroken Worship & Heritage!
hiddenArtifacts.storyUnlocked: Unlike the other six early churches in Kerala that were relocated or rebuilt on new sites over the millennia, Palayoor Church still stands on its original 52 AD plot—preserving ancient granite oil lamps (Kalvilakku) and weathered sculptures!
hiddenArtifacts.stoneKeyMeaning: Standing on its original site in Palayoor for nearly two millennia

hiddenArtifacts.riddleToFind: The white-and-gold Kerala church facade rising beneath the coconut palms.
hiddenArtifacts.hintDirection: Click marker #3 on the main church sanctuary building.
hiddenArtifacts.foundTitle: Where Is It Modern Day Now? Palayoor (Near Guruvayur), Kerala
hiddenArtifacts.storyUnlocked: Every July on Dukrana (the July 3 Feast of St. Thomas), thousands of pilgrims walk the "Thoma Margam" procession to Palayoor in central Kerala, lighting oil lamps and praying in historic East Syriac and Malayalam.
hiddenArtifacts.stoneKeyMeaning: Modern-day central Kerala town housing the 52 AD St. Thomas Pilgrim Church

stops.title: The Cave Refuge & Palm Print in the Rock
stops.subtitle: Step inside the granite cave of Little Mount where St. Thomas prayed and struck a spring from stone
stops.imageCaption: Rock-cut prayer cave and 16th-century chapel at Little Mount (Chinnamalai), Saidapet, Chennai, India.
stops.whatYouCanSeeToday: In the Saidapet neighborhood of southern Chennai, Tamil Nadu, you can stoop through the narrow granite cleft inside the 1551 Portuguese Chapel of Our Lady of Good Health to enter St. Thomas’s actual prayer cave, touch his palm print in the rock window, and see the perennial natural spring on the hillock outside.
stops.didYouKnowHighlight: Even in the blazing summer heat of Chennai when surrounding wells run dry, the tiny rock fissure outside the Little Mount cave—"St. Thomas’s Fountain," which tradition says he struck with his staff for thirsty listeners—still holds cool water!
stops.saintQuote: “Let us also go, that we may die with Him.” — St. Thomas (John 11:16)

globePlacement.regionLabel: Adyar River, Southern Chennai, Coromandel Coast

stops.detectiveCaseTitle: Case #4 · The Granite Cave With the Apostle’s Palm Print & Spring
stops.detectiveLeadPrompt: Crossing to India’s eastern Coromandel Coast, locate the granite hillock beside the Adyar River in southern Chennai where St. Thomas lived in a rock cave and left his handprint in stone!

detectiveClues.headline: A Granite Hillock in Saidapet, Southern Chennai, India
detectiveClues.clueText: Known in Tamil as Chinnamalai ("Little Mount"), this rocky hillock beside the Adyar River in southern Chennai (formerly Madras) encloses a natural rock cavern beneath a 1551 Portuguese vaulted chapel.

detectiveClues.headline: A Handprint in the Rock Window & A Spring Struck from Granite!
detectiveClues.clueText: Inside the cave’s narrow escape tunnel, pilgrims can still see the fossil-like impression of a palm pressed into the granite wall, while outside on the solid rock hilltop sits a natural water fissure that never dries up!

detectiveClues.headline: The Apostle’s Hermitage of Prayer Before His Martyrdom (68–72 AD)
detectiveClues.clueText: During his final years preaching along the eastern coast of Tamilakam, St. Thomas spent nights in fasting and prayer inside this cool rock cave, preaching to crowds gathered around the hillock by day.

hiddenArtifacts.riddleToFind: The candlelit granite altar deep inside the natural rock cavern.
hiddenArtifacts.hintDirection: Click marker #1 in the glowing center of the rock cave.
hiddenArtifacts.foundTitle: St. Thomas’s Cave of Prayer & Fasting (68–72 AD)
hiddenArtifacts.storyUnlocked: After traveling across the southern peninsula to the Coromandel Coast, St. Thomas used this secluded granite cavern beside the Adyar River as his hermitage of silent prayer and teaching.
hiddenArtifacts.stoneKeyMeaning: The granite cavern in southern Chennai where St. Thomas prayed in solitude

hiddenArtifacts.riddleToFind: The narrow sunlit rock cleft on the side of the cave wall.
hiddenArtifacts.hintDirection: Click marker #2 on the sunlit rock opening on the right wall.
hiddenArtifacts.foundTitle: Did You Know? The Palm Print & The Perennial Rock Spring!
hiddenArtifacts.storyUnlocked: When hostile assailants cornered him inside the cave, tradition records that Thomas escaped through this narrow rock opening—leaving his right palm print pressed into the stone—and fled two miles south to Great Mount (St. Thomas Mount).
hiddenArtifacts.stoneKeyMeaning: Preserved inside the narrow rock escape cleft at Little Mount

hiddenArtifacts.riddleToFind: The rough-hewn stone steps leading from the 1551 Portuguese chapel into the cavern.
hiddenArtifacts.hintDirection: Click marker #3 on the stone entrance steps on the left.
hiddenArtifacts.foundTitle: Where Is It Modern Day Now? Little Mount (Saidapet), Chennai, India
hiddenArtifacts.storyUnlocked: Today, Little Mount has its own station on the Chennai Metro Blue Line in Saidapet! Overlooking the historic 1551 Portuguese cave chapel stands a striking circular modern shrine dedicated to Our Lady of Good Health.
hiddenArtifacts.stoneKeyMeaning: Modern-day neighborhood in southern Chennai where the cave shrine stands today

stops.title: Martyrdom on the Mount & The Tomb by the Sea
stops.subtitle: Stand before San Thome Cathedral Basilica in Mylapore, built directly over St. Thomas’s 72 AD tomb
stops.imageCaption: San Thome Cathedral Basilica on the Bay of Bengal shore in Mylapore, Chennai, India.
stops.whatYouCanSeeToday: Along the Marina beachfront in Mylapore, Chennai, you can enter the snow-white neo-Gothic San Thome Cathedral Basilica and descend into the underground crypt to pray directly beside St. Thomas’s original 1st-century tomb—and climb nearby St. Thomas Mount (Parangi Malai), where he was martyred in 72 AD.
stops.didYouKnowHighlight: Did you know there are only THREE basilicas in the entire world built directly over the tomb of one of Jesus’s Twelve Apostles? St. Peter’s Basilica in Rome (St. Peter), Santiago de Compostela in Spain (St. James), and San Thome Basilica in Chennai, India (St. Thomas)!
stops.saintQuote: “Jesus said to him: ‘I am the Way, and the Truth, and the Life.’” — Spoken in answer to St. Thomas (John 14:5–6)

globePlacement.regionLabel: Mylapore Coast, Bay of Bengal, Chennai, India

stops.detectiveCaseTitle: Case #5 · One of Only Three Apostolic Tomb Basilicas on Earth
stops.detectiveLeadPrompt: Only three churches on earth stand directly over the original tomb of one of the Twelve Apostles: Rome, Santiago de Compostela, and this seaside neighborhood of peacocks on the Bay of Bengal!

detectiveClues.headline: A White Neo-Gothic Basilica on the Marina Coast of Chennai, India
detectiveClues.clueText: Anciently called Mayilappur ("Town of Peacocks"), this historic seaside district in central Chennai faces the Bay of Bengal and is crowned by the 1896 white spire of San Thome Cathedral Basilica.

detectiveClues.headline: One of Only Three Basilicas in the World Over an Apostle’s Tomb!
detectiveClues.clueText: Alongside St. Peter’s in the Vatican and St. James in Compostela, Spain, this basilica in Chennai is one of only three churches on the planet built directly over the first-century burial tomb of an Apostle! Even Marco Polo visited it in 1292!

detectiveClues.headline: Martyred with a Lance at St. Thomas Mount on July 3, 72 AD
detectiveClues.clueText: On July 3, 72 AD, while praying before a stone cross carved on nearby Parangi Malai (St. Thomas Mount), the 72-year-old Apostle was pierced with a lance, and his disciples buried his body in this seaside sanctuary of Mylapore.

hiddenArtifacts.riddleToFind: The soaring white spire of San Thome Basilica rising over the tomb crypt.
hiddenArtifacts.hintDirection: Click marker #1 on the tall white basilica spire.
hiddenArtifacts.foundTitle: Martyrdom on July 3, 72 AD & Burial in Mylapore
hiddenArtifacts.storyUnlocked: Pierced with a lance while praying on St. Thomas Mount on July 3, 72 AD, the Apostle’s body was carried by his disciples to the small chapel he had built by the beach in Mylapore and laid to rest in a brick tomb.
hiddenArtifacts.stoneKeyMeaning: The feast of St. Thomas’s martyrdom at St. Thomas Mount and burial in Mylapore

hiddenArtifacts.riddleToFind: The subterranean crypt level beneath the cathedral nave.
hiddenArtifacts.hintDirection: Click marker #2 near the lower sanctuary arches.
hiddenArtifacts.foundTitle: Did You Know? Visited by King Alfred’s Envoys (883 AD) & Marco Polo (1292)!
hiddenArtifacts.storyUnlocked: Long before European colonial ships arrived, Anglo-Saxon King Alfred the Great sent alms all the way from England to St. Thomas’s tomb in India in 883 AD (recorded in the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle), and Marco Polo prayed here in 1292!
hiddenArtifacts.stoneKeyMeaning: Alongside Rome (St. Peter) and Compostela (St. James), built over an Apostle’s tomb

hiddenArtifacts.riddleToFind: The waves of the Bay of Bengal lapping the Mylapore shore.
hiddenArtifacts.hintDirection: Click marker #3 along the coastal garden and sea breeze.
hiddenArtifacts.foundTitle: Where Is It Modern Day Now? San Thome (Mylapore), Chennai, India
hiddenArtifacts.storyUnlocked: Today in Mylapore, Chennai, pilgrims descend into the underground crypt beneath San Thome Basilica to pray before the first-century tomb, and view the ancient lance head and earthen relics in the cathedral museum.
hiddenArtifacts.stoneKeyMeaning: The coastal neighborhood of Mylapore in Chennai where the Basilica stands today

stops.title: The Adriatic Basilica of the Apostle’s Relics
stops.subtitle: Cross back to Italy’s Adriatic coast where St. Thomas’s relics arrived by ship in 1258 AD
stops.eraLabel: 1258 AD to Present · Resting Place of the Relics
stops.imageCaption: Basilica of St. Thomas the Apostle overlooking the Adriatic Sea in Ortona, Abruzzo, Italy.
stops.whatYouCanSeeToday: On a sun-drenched cliff overlooking the Adriatic Sea in Ortona (Abruzzo region, eastern Italy), you can visit the Basilica Concattedrale di San Tommaso Apostolo and descend into the gilded crypt beneath the high altar where the major relics of St. Thomas rest inside a bronze urn.
stops.didYouKnowHighlight: How did St. Thomas’s relics travel from India to Italy? First carried along the Silk Road from Mylapore to Edessa (modern Urfa) in the 3rd century and later to the Greek island of Chios, they were brought across the Adriatic to Ortona on September 6, 1258 by naval captain Leone Acciaiuoli!
stops.saintQuote: “Lord, we do not know where You are going; how can we know the way?” — St. Thomas (John 14:5)

globePlacement.regionLabel: Trabocchi Coast, Adriatic Sea, Abruzzo, Italy

stops.detectiveCaseTitle: Case #6 · The Adriatic Cliffside Port That Guards the Apostle’s Relics
stops.detectiveLeadPrompt: After traveling from Mylapore to Edessa and the Greek island of Chios, a naval captain in 1258 AD carried St. Thomas’s relics across the sea to which cliffside port on Italy’s eastern Adriatic coast?

detectiveClues.headline: A Cliffside Port on the Adriatic “Trabocchi Coast” of Abruzzo, Italy
detectiveClues.clueText: Perched above the blue Adriatic Sea in eastern Italy’s Abruzzo region (province of Chieti), this coastal town is crowned by a medieval Aragonese Castle and the domed Basilica of St. Thomas the Apostle.

detectiveClues.headline: Saved Through a 1566 Siege & Rebuilt After World War II!
detectiveClues.clueText: Brought here from the Aegean island of Chios by Captain Leone Acciaiuoli on September 6, 1258, St. Thomas’s relics and original marble tombstone from Chios survived both a 1566 Ottoman naval raid and the 1943 World War II battle that destroyed the upper church!

detectiveClues.headline: From Mylapore to Edessa, Chios, and Ortona (232–1258 AD)
detectiveClues.clueText: While his original burial crypt remains revered in Mylapore, India (along with relic fragments in Kerala), the major skeletal relics of St. Thomas have rested in the crypt of this Italian Adriatic basilica since 1258 AD.

hiddenArtifacts.riddleToFind: The copper-domed Basilica of St. Thomas rising above the coastal town.
hiddenArtifacts.hintDirection: Click marker #1 on the domed Basilica of St. Thomas.
hiddenArtifacts.foundTitle: September 6, 1258: Arrival of the Apostle’s Relics by Sea
hiddenArtifacts.storyUnlocked: On September 6, 1258, Ortonese naval captain Leone Acciaiuoli returned from the Aegean island of Chios bearing the skeletal relics of St. Thomas and the Greek-inscribed chalcedony slab ("Hagios Thomas"), welcomed by torchlight procession at the harbor.
hiddenArtifacts.stoneKeyMeaning: How St. Thomas’s relics were brought by ship from Chios to Ortona in 1258 AD

hiddenArtifacts.riddleToFind: The cliffside Aragonese Castle watching over the Adriatic harbor.
hiddenArtifacts.hintDirection: Click marker #2 on the coastal fortress overlooking the sea.
hiddenArtifacts.foundTitle: Did You Know? The Relics Were Hidden Wall-Deep in 1943!
hiddenArtifacts.storyUnlocked: During the fierce December 1943 Battle of Ortona in World War II, the parish priest bricked St. Thomas’s bronze reliquary urn inside the bell-tower wall—saving the Apostle’s bones intact even when the cathedral nave collapsed around them!
hiddenArtifacts.stoneKeyMeaning: How the Apostle’s urn and Greek marble slab survived World War II intact

hiddenArtifacts.riddleToFind: The golden harbor promenade curving along the Adriatic Sea.
hiddenArtifacts.hintDirection: Click marker #3 along the sunlit coastal harbor.
hiddenArtifacts.foundTitle: Where Is It Modern Day Now? Ortona, Abruzzo, Italy
hiddenArtifacts.storyUnlocked: Today in Ortona (on Italy’s eastern Adriatic coast, 2.5 hours east of Rome), pilgrims from India and around the world gather in the gilded crypt beneath the rebuilt Basilica of St. Thomas, especially during the annual Perdono festival each May!
hiddenArtifacts.stoneKeyMeaning: The modern Italian Adriatic port where St. Thomas’s relics rest today

trailSubtitle: 3 Stops · Zaragoza Birthplace, Coimbra Miracle of the Roses & Estremoz Peacemaking
globeHeaderSubtitle: Sacred Trails of St. Elizabeth of Portugal (Zaragoza, Coimbra & Estremoz)
completionSummary: You rode straight between drawn royal armies with St. Elizabeth of Portugal—the fearless "Peacemaker Queen" whose legendary winter apron of bread turned into blooming roses and who twice stopped civil wars by riding unarmed onto the battlefield.

stops.title: Aragonese Princess Named for a Saint
stops.subtitle: Sweep your lantern across Caesaraugusta (Aljafería Palace, Zaragoza) to uncover 3 hidden memories
stops.imageCaption: Warm golden Mudéjar palace arches in sunny Zaragoza framing a bright young Spanish princess sharing sweet figs and coins with smiling courtyard servants.
stops.whatYouCanSeeToday: Zaragoza’s UNESCO-listed Aljafería Palace still preserves the historic birth chamber of Portugal’s beloved "Rainha Santa" (Holy Queen).
stops.didYouKnowHighlight: Even before turning twenty, Queen Elizabeth established Portugal’s earliest royal hospitals, shelters for abandoned infants, and free hostels for weary pilgrims walking toward Santiago de Compostela!

detectiveClues.headline: Courage at the Farmhouse of Le Ferriere
detectiveClues.clueText: Just weeks after her joyful First Holy Communion in June 1902, eleven-year-old Maria was sitting on the outdoor stone landing of the shared farmhouse at Le Ferriere mending a shirt while her mother threshed beans in the courtyard below. Suddenly, the troubled nineteen-year-old neighbor boy Alessandro Serenelli tried to assault her—yet courageous Maria stood firm in self-respect and dignity, crying out, *"No! It is a sin! God does not want it!"* Even after he stabbed her fourteen times in panic, her very first thought in the ambulance wasn’t anger—it was asking if her mother was okay!

stops.title: Forest Crosses & Easter Baptism at Caughnawaga
stops.subtitle: Sweep your lantern across Caughnawaga (Castle Village, Mohawk Valley) to uncover 3 hidden memories
stops.imageCaption: Hushed sunlit emerald woodland clearing beside a sparkling spring where a young Indigenous woman gently ties two cedar twigs into a small cross against a tall pine tree.
stops.whatYouCanSeeToday: At the **National Saint Kateri Tekakwitha Shrine** in Fonda, New York, archaeologists uncovered the actual footprint of Caughnawaga’s longhouses—the ONLY completely excavated Iroquois village site from Kateri’s lifetime!
stops.didYouKnowHighlight: Because Kateri found God so intimately in rivers, forests, birds, and maple trees, Pope Benedict XVI named her a beloved **Patron Saint of Ecology and the Environment** alongside St. Francis of Assisi!
stops.saintQuote: I am not my own; I have given myself entirely to Jesus.

Because her uncle fiercely opposed her new faith, Kateri was teased, denied Sunday dinner, and even had stones thrown at her—yet she calmly slipped into the quiet maple woods, tied small wooden crosses to tree bark, and prayed listening to the wind and birds.

On the very same day in 1257, both friends received their doctorates together—Aquinas illuminating faith through crystal-clear reason, and Bonaventure illuminating faith through fiery Franciscan love and beauty. Once when Aquinas visited Bonaventure’s room asking to see the secret library behind his sublime writings, Bonaventure simply pulled back a curtain and pointed quietly to his wooden crucifix!

stops.imageCaption: Breezy green Mediterranean headland glowing in golden sunlight where whitewashed stone cliff hermitages and a coastal lighthouse sanctuary look out over sparkling sapphire waves.
stops.whatYouCanSeeToday: Perched dramatically above the waves of Haifa Bay, **Stella Maris Monastery** ("Star of the Sea") welcomes pilgrims to pray right above the ancient Cave of Elijah.
stops.didYouKnowHighlight: The Hebrew name **Karmel** literally means **"God’s Orchard"**—and Mount Carmel’s coastal lighthouse beside Stella Maris inspired sailors for centuries to call Mary *Stella Maris*, guiding ships safely home!
stops.saintQuote: Flower of Carmel, tall vine blossom-laden, Star of the Sea.

stops.title: The Brown Scapular Vision at Aylesford, Kent

stops.imageCaption: Peaceful sunlit English medieval stone priory courtyard beside a gentle winding river where a radiant gentle Mother extends a humble brown wool scapular to a kneeling elderly friar.
stops.whatYouCanSeeToday: Restored by returning Carmelites in 1949, historic **Aylesford Priory (The Friars)** in Kent welcomes hundreds of thousands of visitors yearly to its glowing ceramic chapels, peaceful rose gardens, and medieval river walls!
stops.didYouKnowHighlight: A "scapular" was originally just a practical brown cloth work-apron worn over a monk’s shoulders while gardening and washing dishes—so wearing a tiny Brown Scapular quietly reminds ordinary people that everyday work belongs to Mary and Jesus!
stops.saintQuote: Receive this sign of my motherly protection and peace.

hiddenArtifacts.storyUnlocked: Forced by wars in the Holy Land to sail west to Europe in the 1230s, the newborn Carmelite brothers struggled to find acceptance in England—until their gentle elderly leader **St. Simon Stock** cried out in heartfelt prayer at **Aylesford Priory** in Kent: *"Flower of Carmel, grant a sign of your favor!"* Tradition cherishes July 16, 1251 as the day Our Lady appeared holding the humble **Brown Scapular**—a simple protective garment of motherly closeness symbolizing belonging completely to Jesus through Mary.

stops.title: Leaving a Golden Senator’s Villa on Aventine Hill
stops.subtitle: Sweep your lantern across Mons Aventinus, Roma to uncover 3 hidden memories
stops.imageCaption: Serene sunset view over ancient cypress-lined Roman hilltop marble villas overlooking the winding golden Tiber River.
stops.whatYouCanSeeToday: Rome’s tranquil Aventine Hill remains one of the quietest, most luminous corners of the Eternal City—still overlooking the river toward Ostia.
stops.didYouKnowHighlight: St. Alexis’s unforgettable story inspired the **Chanson de Saint Alexis** (c. 1040)—one of the very first great literary poems ever written in the French language!
stops.saintQuote: True riches begin the moment you no longer need to be admired.

stops.title: Seventeen Years Among Beggars in Edessa
stops.subtitle: Sweep your lantern across Edessa, Mesopotamia to uncover 3 hidden memories
stops.imageCaption: Warm ochre sandstone church colonnade in ancient Mesopotamia where a ragged smiling stranger gently hands away his own freshly begged copper coins to hungry children.
stops.whatYouCanSeeToday: In Eastern Christian tradition—Syriac, Greek, and Slavic alike—St. Alexis is cherished above all by his ancient Edessa title: **St. Alexius, the Man of God**!
stops.didYouKnowHighlight: Remarkably, the earliest 5th-century Syriac biography of the "Man of God" was written right in Edessa within living memory of his quiet life on the church steps!
stops.saintQuote: Blessed is the soul known only to God.

hiddenArtifacts.foundTitle: Seventeen Years Among Beggars in Edessa
hiddenArtifacts.storyUnlocked: Arriving penniless in the ancient Syrian city of Edessa, Alexis sat quietly for seventeen years on the stone steps of the Church of Our Lady—sharing almost every coin people dropped into his bowl with needier beggars while praying through the night! Even when his father’s servants traveled east searching for him and dropped alms right into his palm, they didn’t recognize their master’s sun-weathered son. When townsfolk finally began honoring him as a living saint, humble Alexis quietly boarded a ship again to avoid fame—only for Mediterranean gales to blow his ship straight back to Italy!

stops.eraLabel: c. 864 BC · Mount Horeb / Mount Sinai, Egypt

stops.whatYouCanSeeToday: Right along the climb up Egypt’s Mount Sinai sits the serene stone **Chapel of Prophet Elijah** in Elijah’s Basin—built beside the ancient cave where the burned-out prophet learned to hear God’s whisper.
stops.didYouKnowHighlight: Elijah’s story under the broom tree is one of the Bible’s sweetest self-care moments: when Elijah felt completely defeated, God’s first prescription wasn’t a sermon—it was **a snack, cool water, and two good naps!**

hiddenArtifacts.foundTitle: The Still Small Voice on Mount Horeb (Sinai)
hiddenArtifacts.storyUnlocked: Even the bravest hero gets burnt out! Fleeing death threats from Queen Jezebel right after his Mount Carmel triumph, exhausted Elijah collapsed under a desert broom tree whispering, *"Enough, Lord!"* Gently, an angel didn’t lecture him—instead the angel let him take a **nap** and baked him warm hearth-bread with cool water! Restored, Elijah walked forty days to **Mount Horeb (Sinai)**—where roaring wind shattered rocks, an earthquake shook the cliff, and wildfire blazed past… yet God wasn’t in any of the noise! Instead, God met Elijah in a **tiny, whispering silence** (*"a still, small voice"*).

stops.title: Collecting Desert Wisdom in Egypt & Bethlehem
stops.subtitle: Sweep your lantern across Scetis & Kellia, Egypt to uncover 3 hidden memories
stops.imageCaption: Warm amber Egyptian desert oasis at twilight where two earnest young pilgrim-friends sit by an oil lamp eagerly taking notes from a smiling elderly Desert Father.
stops.whatYouCanSeeToday: Cassian’s sparkling interviews—*The Conferences*—remain one of the most readable, psychologically insightful spiritual classics ever written!
stops.didYouKnowHighlight: Ever wondered where the famous list of **"Seven Deadly Sins"** originally came from? stops.saintQuote: O God, come to my assistance; O Lord, make haste to help me.

stops.subtitle: Sweep your lantern across Abbaye Saint-Victor, Massilia to uncover 3 hidden memories
stops.eraLabel: c. 415 – 435 · Abbey of Saint-Victor, Marseille, France
stops.imageCaption: Weathered golden limestone fortress-abbey overlooking the sparkling turquoise Old Port of Marseille bathed in bright Provençal Mediterranean sunlight.
stops.whatYouCanSeeToday: Overlooking Marseille’s glittering Vieux-Port, visitors can step right down into the hushed 5th-century stone crypt of **Saint-Victor Abbey** where St. John Cassian’s sarcophagus rests!
stops.didYouKnowHighlight: St. Benedict of Nursia loved John Cassian so much that he explicitly commanded in the *Rule of St. Benedict* that monks read Cassian’s *Conferences* aloud every evening after supper—shaping 1,500 years of Western civilization!
stops.saintQuote: Hold fast to one short verse of prayer in every moment, and peace will anchor your heart.

completionSummary: You crossed all of Europe from sparkling Swedish lakes to sunny Rome and Jerusalem with St. Bridget of Sweden—Co-Patroness of Europe, happily married mother of eight, fearless speaker of truth to popes and kings, and founder of the Bridgettine Order.

stops.subtitle: Sweep your lantern across Vadstena Kloster, Östergötland to uncover 3 hidden memories
stops.imageCaption: Peaceful pale blue-grey medieval stone abbey standing beside sparkling northern Swedish lake waters framed by golden birch trees and crisp sunlit skies.
stops.whatYouCanSeeToday: Vadstena’s soaring blue-limestone **Abbey Church** (built from Bridget’s own architectural instructions!) still guards her golden shrine beside shimmering Lake Vättern.
stops.didYouKnowHighlight: St. Bridget was a joyful champion of equal partnership in marriage and leadership—and her daughter **St. Catherine of Sweden** became her closest lifelong travel buddy and first Abbess of Vadstena!
stops.saintQuote: Lord, show me the way, and make me willing to follow it.

stops.title: Fearless Voice for Peace at Piazza Farnese, Rome
stops.subtitle: Sweep your lantern across Piazza Farnese, Roma to uncover 3 hidden memories
stops.eraLabel: 1349 – July 23, 1373 · Casa di Santa Brigida, Rome
stops.imageCaption: Warm ochre Renaissance Roman palazzo overlooking a sunlit marble fountain piazza where an elderly Nordic noblewoman writes fearless urgent letters while feeding grateful Roman beggars outside.
stops.whatYouCanSeeToday: Right on Rome’s gorgeous **Piazza Farnese**, the **Casa di Santa Brigida** welcomes travelers from every nation into St. Bridget’s preserved sunlit rooms, charming church, and famous rooftop terrace!
stops.didYouKnowHighlight: In 1999, Pope St. John Paul II named St. Bridget of Sweden one of the three female **Co-Patronesses of Europe** (alongside St. Catherine of Siena and St. Edith Stein) for uniting Northern and Southern Europe!
stops.saintQuote: There is no one so weak that God cannot make them strong for peace.

Amazingly, both Pope Urban V and Pope Gregory XI listened—and Rome welcomed the Papacy home!

stops.whatYouCanSeeToday: Today **St. Maron Monastery in Annaya** is one of the Middle East’s most vibrant pilgrimage sanctuaries—visited every year by over 4 million Christians, Muslims, and Druze coming side by side to pray for healing and peace!

hiddenArtifacts.storyUnlocked: Ordained a priest in 1859, Father Charbel lived sixteen humble years at the **Monastery of St. Maron in Annaya**, working joyfully in the vineyards, baking bread, and celebrating the ancient Aramaic Maronite Liturgy with deep reverence. Astonished by the quiet sign, his abbot finally granted Charbel’s longtime dream: permission to live up on the mountain peak as a hermit!

stops.title: "Son of Thunder" on the Sea of Galilee & Mount Tabor
stops.subtitle: Sweep your lantern across Lacus Tiberiadis (Sea of Galilee) to uncover 3 hidden memories
stops.eraLabel: c. 28 – 30 AD · Capernaum & Mount Tabor, Galilee
stops.imageCaption: Sparkling sunlit turquoise waters of the Sea of Galilee framed by wooden fishing boats and green hills where two eager young brothers drop their nets immediately at Jesus’s beckoning smile.
stops.whatYouCanSeeToday: Along the peaceful basalt shoreline of Capernaum and atop rounded **Mount Tabor**, pilgrims remember how Jesus transformed a fiery young "Son of Thunder" into a fearless witness of love.
stops.didYouKnowHighlight: Why is he called St. James **"the Greater"**? Not because he was more important, simply because he was **taller or older** than the other Apostle named James (St. James the Less)!
stops.saintQuote: Can you drink the cup that I am going to drink? They said to Him: We can!

hiddenArtifacts.storyUnlocked: Mending heavy fishing nets beside his father Zebedee and younger brother John along the sunny shores of the **Sea of Galilee**, bold young **James** dropped everything the instant Jesus called his name! Fiery, passionate, and sometimes way too hot-headed—Jesus playfully nicknamed James and John **"Boanerges" ("Sons of Thunder")** after they asked if they should call lightning down on an unfriendly village!—yet Jesus brought James into His closest inner circle of three (Peter, James, and John) to witness Jairus’s daughter raised to life, the dazzling **Transfiguration on Mount Tabor**, and the lonely Agony in Gethsemane.

stops.title: Our Lady of the Pillar Along the Ebro in Zaragoza
stops.subtitle: Sweep your lantern across Caesaraugusta (Basílica del Pilar, Zaragoza) to uncover 3 hidden memories
stops.imageCaption: Starlit tranquil riverbanks of the broad Ebro River in Spain illuminated by a gentle radiant pillar of jasper light comforting a discouraged, travel-worn Galilean apostle.
stops.whatYouCanSeeToday: Rising gloriously beside the Ebro River with eleven colorful tiled domes, Zaragoza’s **Basílica de Nuestra Señora del Pilar** houses the venerated jasper pillar—revered as the oldest Marian shrine in history!
stops.didYouKnowHighlight: Notice how wonderfully human this tradition is: even a giant Apostle felt discouraged and wanted to quit—and needed a warm word of encouragement to keep walking forward!
stops.saintQuote: Stand firm as this pillar; the seed you plant in tears will harvest in joy.

hiddenArtifacts.riddleToFind: Find the luminous focal point of Caesaraugusta (Basílica del Pilar, Zaragoza) in the scene.
hiddenArtifacts.hintDirection: Scan the center-left horizon of the painting.
hiddenArtifacts.foundTitle: Our Lady of the Pillar Along the Ebro in Zaragoza
hiddenArtifacts.storyUnlocked: Ancient Spanish tradition treasures how St. James sailed all the way to the western edge of the Roman Empire—**Hispania**—to bring the Gospel to the ends of the earth! Feeling exhausted and discouraged along the banks of the Ebro River at Caesaraugusta (Zaragoza) after winning barely a handful of converts, James knelt praying in the moonlight on January 2, 40 AD—when Mary (still living in Jerusalem!) appeared standing atop a luminous **jasper pillar**, encouraging him never to give up and promising that faith in Spain would stand firm as stone!

stops.imageCaption: Warm incense-scented ancient stone Jerusalem basilica aglow with hundreds of hanging silver oil lamps illuminating golden Armenian floor tiles.
stops.whatYouCanSeeToday: Hidden behind ancient limestone walls in Jerusalem’s Old City stands the breathtaking **Armenian Cathedral of St. James**, glowing with hundreds of suspended silver lamps over the traditional site of his martyrdom!
stops.didYouKnowHighlight: Of all twelve original Apostles, St. James the Greater is the **ONLY Apostle whose martyrdom is explicitly recorded right inside the New Testament** (Acts 12:1–2)!
stops.saintQuote: Peace be with you, brother!

hiddenArtifacts.foundTitle: First Apostle Martyred in Jerusalem
hiddenArtifacts.storyUnlocked: Returning home to Jerusalem around 44 AD, James kept his bold promise to Jesus—becoming the **very first of the Twelve Apostles to shed his blood as a martyr** under King Herod Agrippa I (Acts 12:2)! Early Church historian Eusebius shares an unforgettable eyewitness detail: the Roman accuser who led James to execution was so blown away by James’s serene courage that he confessed faith in Christ on the spot and asked forgiveness—whereupon smiling James embraced him saying **"Peace be with you!"**, and both received the martyr’s crown together!

detectiveClues.headline: First Apostle Martyred in Jerusalem
detectiveClues.clueText: Returning home to Jerusalem around 44 AD, James kept his bold promise to Jesus—becoming the **very first of the Twelve Apostles to shed his blood as a martyr** under King Herod Agrippa I (Acts 12:2)! Early Church historian Eusebius shares an unforgettable eyewitness detail: the Roman accuser who led James to execution was so blown away by James’s serene courage that he confessed faith in Christ on the spot and asked forgiveness—whereupon smiling James embraced him saying **"Peace be with you!"**, and both received the martyr’s crown together!

stops.subtitle: Sweep your lantern across Nicomedia, Bithynia to uncover 3 hidden memories
stops.imageCaption: Warm golden sunlit ancient Roman port veranda overlooking the sparkling Sea of Marmara where a gentle young court physician opens his wooden medicine box to tend a grateful poor villager free of charge.
stops.whatYouCanSeeToday: In Eastern Christianity, St. Panteleimon is honored as the greatest of the **Holy Unmercenary Healers** (*Anargyroi* — literally "Silverless Doctors" who heal for love, not profit!).
stops.didYouKnowHighlight: Why did jealous rival doctors turn young Pantaleon in to Emperor Diocletian in 305? Because patients kept flocking to the kind young doctor who healed them with BOTH skilled medicine AND warm prayer—without charging them a cent!
stops.saintQuote: Heal every suffering neighbor as freely as God has healed your own heart.

stops.didYouKnowHighlight: Wait—think of that fun trivia nugget next time you get dressed: **St. Pantaleon** (the generous 4th-century doctor!) → Venice’s *San Pantalon* → Venetian comic character *Pantalone* → **"Pantaloons"** → modern **"Pants"**!
stops.saintQuote: True medicine joins skillful hands with a compassionate soul.
